Theme 074 · Characters & mascots

Felt Puppet Show

A tabletop puppet booth: fuzzy felt, ping-pong-ball eyes, a wooden stage lip and a teal velvet curtain. Pulse is a hand puppet with a coral nose who pops up to point at the problem — but only a real human hand can press the button.

readability ●●○trust ●●○effort high
1 · HOOK0:00–0:08

The grumpy puppet sinks in from below the stage lip while paper dashboards flutter down; the placard bobs up on the snare at 0:04 and the head droops on the last beat before the drop.

2 · REVEAL0:08 (drop)

The curtains fly apart on the drop and Pulse shoots up from behind the board (0.25 s, back.out), mouth open; the marquee bulbs chase left-to-right in 16ths and the mark sign swings in on beat 2.

3 · PROOF MOMENT0:12–0:32

Pulse’s mouth flaps on every beat as its rod-arm swings to the easel; the chart line is ‘drawn’ in marker over 2 beats. The human hand enters from the right and presses Roll back on the bar downbeat — the button squashes.

Acme Pulse
Start free
4 · CTA0:36–0:45

Both puppets rise and bow together on beat 1, tagline drops in on the valance, and the felt Start free ticket slaps down on the final hit.

COMPONENT KIT

  • Felt hand puppet — Pulse: teal felt, ping-pong eyes, coral nose (the mark’s dot)
  • Grumpy co-star — grey-lilac puppet with heavy lids = the overwhelmed team
  • Stage booth — velvet curtain, fringed valance, wooden board that hides the hands
  • Placard on a stick — cream card for hook lines and the tagline
  • Marker easel — hand-drawn chart with −18% and the deploy line
  • Real hand + felt button — the human decision, deliberately not a puppet

MOTION · MUSIC

  • Pop-up — puppets rise from behind the board, 0.25 s back.out(1.8) with a 2-frame overshoot hold; always entering on a downbeat
  • Mouth flap — jaw opens on each spoken syllable, locked to 8th notes (0.25 s at 120 BPM); stepped at 12 fps for a hand-performed feel
  • Rod swing — arm rods swing with sine.inOut 0.5 s pendulum overshoot; the button squash is 0.1 s scaleY 1→0.8→1 on the bar downbeat

WHY / RISK · ADAPT IT

Why: Hand-puppet ads have sold products in ten seconds since the 1950s: two contrasting characters and one gag. The puppet can’t press buttons — a built-in, funny way to say the agent flags and the human decides. Risk: High production cost if shot practically, and silliness can undercut a serious incident story — keep the easel data crisp and the puppet’s gag to one beat.

Adapt to your product: Swap the easel for your own screen or chart printed on a card, give your puppet your brand’s accent colour as its nose or tuft, and let a real hand perform your product’s main action.

References: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilkins_Coffee (Jim Henson’s 10-second two-puppet ads (1957–61)) · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muppet (felt-over-foam construction, wide mouths, protruding eyes)
